**Search combines hard requirements with preferences.** “Running shoes under 3000” contains a product intent and a price constraint. A ranking model may trade among relevant eligible shoes, but it should not treat the price ceiling as a soft preference that can be ignored for a high-converting item.

**Follow the query.** Identify product/category terms, preserve model numbers and brands, interpret currency from known locale or clarification, and extract hard filters. Retrieve from lexical and semantic indexes, fuse candidates, enforce current eligibility, then rerank using richer relevance and product signals. Exact lexical matching remains valuable for rare names and identifiers. [3](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/)

**Why two retrieval routes help.** Lexical search can find an exact model code; semantic search can connect “shoes for jogging” with “running footwear.” Each can fail where the other succeeds. Fusion combines candidate lists, while a reranker judges them in the full query context. Raw lexical and embedding scores are not automatically on a comparable scale.

**Freshness can matter more than embedding quality.** Price and stock may change faster than item descriptions or vectors. Revalidate critical filters using current data before showing or selling the item. Training features must still reflect what was known when the historical impression occurred, rather than today's corrected inventory.

Evaluate query relevance, constraint compliance, zero-result rate, completed purchases, cancellations/returns, and latency. A system that boosts purchases by displaying misleading matches can harm user trust. Use relevance judgments and hard-query slices before relying only on aggregate conversion changes.

**Technical details and references.**

Parse the query into text intent and hard filters. For “running shoes under 3000,” infer a local currency only from a known locale or ask; extract the price ceiling as a filter, not merely a ranking feature. Correct spelling conservatively and preserve brand/model tokens. Query both lexical and semantic indexes with availability, geography, and policy constraints, then fuse candidates.

Rerank with relevance, stock/size availability, price, delivery promise, and calibrated purchase likelihood. Purchase logs are exposure-biased; record impressions and positions, avoid treating unseen products as negatives, and use time-based splits. Preserve exact-match relevance so a high-converting unrelated item does not displace the requested product.

Update price/inventory faster than slow catalog embeddings and revalidate critical availability before checkout. Evaluate query-level relevance, filter compliance, zero-result rate, conversion, returns, and latency by head/tail query. Fall back to lexical retrieval if vector search fails. A conversion-only objective can promote misleading products, so include cancellation/return and customer-satisfaction guardrails.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** Reciprocal-rank fusion can combine lexical and dense lists using $score(d)=\sum_r1/(k+rank_r(d))$ under a fixed convention. It avoids directly comparing incompatible raw scores, but the fusion constant and candidate budgets still need tuning. Enforce hard price/availability constraints independently so ranking cannot silently trade them away for predicted conversion. [3](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/)
